messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen

Vignette:
Javier Morales is a 53-year-old tax consultant who came to treatment after months of telling himself he should be able to handle things on his own. He is divorced and lives alone, and when he first described what happened, he did so in a flat, careful way, as if he were trying not to set off something in himself. The assault by police occurred late one evening after a client meeting ran long during tax season. Javier had been driving home through an area he did not know well because of a road closure and was pulled over. He remembers the stop turning chaotic very quickly. He tried to ask why he had been stopped and to explain where he was coming from, but he recalls raised voices, being ordered out of the car, and then being forced down hard enough that he felt sharp pain in his side and shoulder. What has stayed with him most vividly is not a complete sequence but flashes: a face above him, the scrape of pavement, blood on skin, the sight of his own injuries and the injuries on another man nearby who had also been brought to the curb. Those visual fragments still feel immediate to him, as though they belong to the present rather than the past.

In the days afterward, Javier sought medical care for the pain, but he found that the physical sensations themselves became reminders. A stab in his shoulder or soreness along his ribs could make him feel abruptly pulled back to the pavement, his mind filling in the rest before he had time to think. Seeing visible injuries on other people had a similar effect. If a client came into his office with a bandaged hand, or if he passed someone on the street with bruising or stitches, he would feel his attention lock onto the wound and then onto the memory of that night. News stories or passing references to people harmed by police or other violence also struck him with unusual force. He would find himself thinking not abstractly about “victims,” but about specific bodies on the ground, specific faces, and the frightening sense that a person can be reduced in an instant to someone hurt and exposed in public.

Over the following months, Javier’s world became organized around danger. Because the stop had happened in an unfamiliar area, he had come to believe that places he did not know were especially risky because he could not read them in advance. He began refusing invitations that involved new restaurants, unfamiliar office buildings, or meeting clients anywhere but his own workplace. Even when he did go somewhere necessary, he could not settle until he had located exits and imagined how he would leave if something happened. In waiting rooms, conference spaces, and even coffee shops near his office, he scanned for doors, side corridors, and anything that might become a trap. Walking from the parking garage to his building, he repeatedly looked behind him to check whether anyone was following. He knew this made him appear tense and distracted, and a colleague once asked if he was expecting someone. Javier brushed it off, but the question embarrassed him.

At work, these habits narrowed his life in concrete ways. As a tax consultant he had once prided himself on being steady with clients, willing to travel across town, and able to manage stressful deadlines without fuss. Now he steered clients toward phone calls or virtual meetings whenever possible and avoided taking on new accounts if they required him to visit unfamiliar offices. He arranged his chair in meeting rooms so he could see the exit. When pain flared in his shoulder during a consultation, his concentration could break completely, and he would need to excuse himself to the restroom until he felt anchored again. The restrictions were not only practical; they deepened his sense that he no longer moved through the world the way other people did.

Javier speaks often about feeling set apart. Since the assault, he has felt that other people carry on with an ease that is no longer available to him, and he experiences himself as isolated even when he is with others. The divorce preceded the trauma, but living alone now feels heavier to him. He has come to believe there is something about him that made the event happen, something in the way he spoke, looked, or existed in that moment that drew the violence onto him. He returns to tiny details, wondering whether another man would have said less, moved differently, somehow been spared. Alongside that self-blame is a bleakness he finds hard to admit aloud: at his lowest moments he is not sure his life is worth living anymore. He does not describe this dramatically; rather, it appears as a worn-down conviction that his life has become small, watchful, and detached from other people.

What finally brought Javier to seek help was an incident in his office lobby when he saw a delivery driver with a cut across his cheek and, at the same time, felt a sudden ache in his ribs. He became overwhelmed, left the building before his next appointment, and sat in his car checking the rearview mirror again and again before he could drive. Missing the appointment meant disappointing a longstanding client, and for the first time he allowed himself to consider that this was not passing on its own. He came in saying he was tired of arranging every day around what might happen. What frightens him most is the thought that this watchfulness and isolation are now permanent, that he has been marked in some essential way by what happened. What he hopes for, though he says it cautiously, is to feel less cut off from other people and less trapped inside the moment he was thrown to the ground.
